doc.title: Larry Gold interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 18, 2025

title: Baritone sax and cello Bach suites; Anthony Jackson
summary: Playing Bach suites on baritone sax, and bassist Anthony Jackson, who wrote a bass line with Gamble and Huff and practiced Bach.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: Here's a little — why this just occurred to me — the baritone saxophone and the cello, especially a baritone saxophone with a low A and the cello are like this. They have the same range and I had a student here who played one of the Bach unaccompanied cello suites on the baritone saxophone. It was awesome except there's no place to breathe.
That's the problem. Even, I don't know you should — what did he play the first one? I mean do you remember which suite it was?
Yeah she played the first one.

Well she should do a little more research. Because the first one there's one where they say the legato goes all the way through the whole measure. And then there's one where they say the legato goes halfway. So you can actually play it [scats] so you can breathe within that context. So like I said there are all different ways of stroking the kitty. You know? But I admire that. I remember — do you know the name of a bass player named Anthony Jackson?

Very great jazz bass player. He grew up in Philadelphia and he actually wrote "Money Money, Money." He did that bass line with Gamble & Huff. If you go back, I'll bet he made more money from that song than he made from anything in his entire life. Gamble & Huff gave him a piece of the song, because he came up with that [scats] — whatever it was, I can't remember it and I can't sing it exactly. But one morning I came in to the studio and he was there and I hear [scats]. He was practicing the first Bach suite. This was like 1973. I looked at him and I said, "Man." He said "I love it."
